A.explanation: Force has magnitude and direction, for example $F = ma$ acts in the direction of acceleration, so it is a vector.

B.explanation: Momentum $p = mv$ has the same direction as velocity, so it needs direction and is a vector.

C.explanation: Velocity is speed in a stated direction, so it has magnitude and direction and is a vector.

D.explanation: Work $W = Fd\cos\theta$ is energy transferred with magnitude only and no direction, so it is a scalar.

hints: Ask of each of force, momentum, velocity and work whether you must give a direction as well as a magnitude to describe it fully.
Recall how direction enters $F = ma$ and $p = mv$, where acceleration and velocity give the force and momentum a direction.
Write work for a constant force as $W = Fd\cos\theta$ using only the component of force along displacement and decide if the energy transferred has a direction.
walkthrough: Recall the test: a scalar has magnitude only, while a vector has magnitude and direction.
Force is a vector because a push or pull of given size must act in a direction, as in $F = ma$.
Momentum $p = mv$ is a vector because mass is scalar but velocity $v$ has direction, so $p$ has the direction of $v$. Velocity itself is speed in a direction, so it is also a vector.
Work is defined by $W = Fd\cos\theta$, the product of force magnitude and displacement magnitude with $\cos\theta$ selecting the component along the motion.
The result is an amount of energy transferred, measured in joules with magnitude only and no direction, so work is a scalar. This is option D.
